qt: to the Commission Georgios Aftias (PPE) Subject:

Based on the communications issued by the Commission in 2026, there is fiscal space for actions to address high fuel and energy prices. Targeted subsidies for vulnerable households and support for businesses that have been especially hard hit by the energy crisis should be key tools in addressing this problem. The Commission has already allocated EUR 14.5 billion for measures to address the 2026 energy price shock. At the same time, the new European fiscal framework provides for the possibility of triggering an escape clause, which would allow for a temporary deviation from the agreed fiscal requirements in exceptional circumstances when there is a severe impact on public finances, provided that there is no threat to debt sustainability. Europe cannot be a passive bystander. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

Does it intend, in view of persistent rising prices and high energy costs, to allow additional budgetary flexibility for Member States so that they can provide energy subsidies and direct payments to households, pensioners and small and medium-sized enterprises?
Is it considering triggering a special fiscal clause to address high prices and the energy crisis if high prices persist?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (25.11.2026) On 5 June 2026, the Commission announced that Member States could request to broaden the scope of the National Escape Clause for defence to include energy security measures1. This broadening provides Member States extra flexibility for handling significant upfront costs to ensure Europe's long-term energy security. Any measures benefiting from this flexibility must make a direct contribution to accelerating the energy transition and reduce the dependency on fossil fuels 2. To ensure continued fiscal sustainability, the scale of overall flexibility is capped and integrated into the existing framework for fiscal surveillance. In addition, the new fiscal framework already contains various elements of flexibility to allow Member States to partly cater for the current situation, as it allows fiscal policy to be countercyclical. For instance, in the short run, Member States do not need to compensate for revenue shortfalls due to an economic slowdown nor increasing interest expenditure, which is clearly relevant at the moment. Outside the flexibility for defence and energy security measures, it is important that Member States continue to stick to the fiscal requirements as set in their medium-term fiscal structural plans or in Council recommendations issued under the excessive deficit procedure. Along with higher price pressures, the yields in the global sovereign debt markets have been increasing in recent weeks, as well as the spreads within the euro area. Now is therefore the time to remain prudent and uphold the rules-based fiscal framework, thereby rebuilding fiscal buffers.
1 See Commission communication on the 2026 Spring Package (COM (2026) 200 final) https://reforms-

investments.ec.europa.eu/publications-0/2026-european-semester-spring-package-communication_en. 2 See Commission Notice on Guidance to Member States on Broadening the Scope of the National Escape Clause for Energy Security (C/2026/4514) https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/C/2026/4514/oj/eng.
